questions.q: Define technological intelligence and list three specific skills it emphasises according to the NCERT textbook.
questions.a: Technological intelligence is the form of intelligence promoted in technologically advanced societies, emphasising skills of attention, observation, analysis, performance, speed, and achievement orientation. Three specific skills: (1) analytical reasoning, (2) rapid information processing, (3) abstract symbolic manipulation. A wrong answer that lists only "problem-solving" or "logical thinking" without the cultural context (speed, achievement orientation) reveals the student has memorised a generic definition but misses the culturally specific valuation that distinguishes technological intelligence from other forms.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the Sanskrit term *buddhi* is described as having a broader scope than the Western concept of intelligence.
questions.a: *Buddhi* includes cognitive components (knowledge, discrimination, understanding) but also integrates affective components (feelings, opinions, self-knowledge based on conscience, will, desire) and motivational components (determined action, mental effort). Western intelligence focuses primarily on cognitive parameters. If a student says "*buddhi* just means wisdom" or equates it only with "emotional intelligence", they are oversimplifying and missing the explicit NCERT breakdown of four competencies (cognitive, social, emotional, entrepreneurial) that together constitute integral intelligence.

questions.q: A researcher administers a standard Western verbal IQ test (heavy on vocabulary and abstract analogies) to two groups: urban Indian students educated in English-medium schools and rural Indian students educated in vernacular-medium schools. The urban group scores significantly higher. Using the concept of culture-fair vs. culture-biased tests, explain why this result does NOT necessarily mean the urban group is more intelligent.
questions.a: The test is culture-biased: its items reflect urban, middle-class, English-speaking cultural experiences (vocabulary, abstract analogies) that are more familiar to the urban group. The rural group’s intelligence may be equally high but expressed through different cultural tools (e.g., practical agricultural knowledge, oral reasoning, social negotiation). A culture-fair test would use non-verbal items (e.g., Raven’s Progressive Matrices) or experiences common to both cultures. If the student attributes the score difference solely to innate ability, they confuse test bias with actual intelligence differences — a classic misconception that leads to mislabeling disadvantaged groups as "less intelligent".

questions.q: Compare and contrast the four competencies of integral intelligence (*buddhi*) with the three components of Sternberg’s triarchic theory. Identify two similarities and two differences.
questions.a: Similarities: (1) Both go beyond pure cognitive/analytical ability — *buddhi* includes social/emotional/entrepreneurial; Sternberg includes experiential (creative) and contextual (practical). (2) Both view intelligence as adaptive to environment. Differences: (1) *Buddhi* explicitly includes moral/ethical dimensions (honesty, respect for elders, self-evaluation) while Sternberg’s components are amoral cognitive styles. (2) *Buddhi*’s entrepreneurial competence (persistence, vigilance, goal-directedness) maps loosely to contextual intelligence but adds a motivational/volitional layer absent in Sternberg’s description. A student who only lists components without analysing the moral/motivational distinction shows surface-level comparison.

questions.q: Critique the statement: "To make intelligence tests fair for all Indian students, we should simply translate Western tests into Hindi and other regional languages."
questions.a: Translation alone does not remove cultural bias because (1) item content may still reflect Western cultural experiences (e.g., vocabulary about snow, subways, or abstract analogies unfamiliar in rural India), (2) the underlying construct (technological intelligence) may not align with *buddhi*’s emphasis on social/emotional/entrepreneurial competence, and (3) norms derived from Western populations misrepresent Indian performance distributions. A proper culture-fair approach requires redefining the construct, developing items from Indian cultural contexts, and establishing Indian norms. If a student agrees with the statement, they confuse linguistic equivalence with cultural equivalence — a fundamental error in cross-cultural assessment.

questions.q: Design a brief scenario (3-4 sentences) depicting a person demonstrating high *buddhi* but low technological intelligence. Explicitly label which of the four *buddhi* competencies are shown.
questions.a: Example: "Meera, a 60-year-old village elder, cannot solve abstract logical puzzles quickly (low technological intelligence). However, she mediates caste disputes with deep empathy and fairness (social competence), regulates her anger during heated arguments (emotional competence), persists in organising annual flood-relief efforts despite setbacks (entrepreneurial competence), and discriminates which medicinal herbs suit each villager’s ailment (cognitive competence)." A good answer must show all four competencies in a culturally grounded context. A poor answer might only show one competency or use a Western-style "street smart" example that actually reflects contextual intelligence rather than *buddhi*’s moral-social integration.
